children.text: This Software Requirements Specification (SRS) document defines the requirements for the volunteer management system (VMS), a new product that can organize volunteers and requests for them so seniors and students looking for support can be helped more efficiently
Project managers should read sections 1 and 2. Developers should refer to section 2, particularly the use cases and user requirements to support development of the product.
Any section which has not been completed in the current iteration of the project will be marked as TBD

This document details the software requirements specification for the Volunteer Management System version 1.0. It is intended to help developers have a clear idea of the system functions and help project managers understand the user requirements.
User classes are classified as Direct or Indirect, and as Favoured, Disfavoured, or Ignored.
Use case IDs use the format UC-#; preconditions, postconditions, and exceptions are labelled PRE-#, POST-#, and E#.
Dates use DD/MM/YYYY.
"TBD" marks information not yet available.
Please refer to the linked vision and scope document

The Volunteer Management System (VMS) is a new product that is intended to organize volunteers and requests for them to more efficiently help seniors who need support. The VMS interfaces with a government system to validate police background checks of volunteers before they are approved for the VMS.

Use Case 3

ID and Name:

UC-3 Create New Volunteer

Author:

Jay Erickson

Date Created:

18/10/2026

Primary Actor:

Volunteer

Secondary Actors:

System Administrator

Description:

Create a new volunteer profile to add to the VMS. This profile is based on personal information the potential volunteer provides and is entered into the system by a system administrator.

Trigger:

A potential volunteer contacts a system administrator wanting to become a volunteer and provides personal information about themself.

Preconditions:

None

Postconditions:

POST-1. A volunteer profile is added to the VMS.

POST-2. The profile awaits approval for police background and required education checks.

Normal Flow:

1.0   Person wants to sign up as a volunteer.

1.1   Person provides personal information to system administrators.

1.2 System Administrator creates a blank volunteer profile

1.3 System Administrator fills in the volunteer profile with information provided by the person.

1.4 Volunteer profile is added to the VMS.

Alternative Flows:

1.1.1 Person provides personal information to the VMS digitally and waits to be approved and officially added to the system later by a system administrator. 

Exceptions:

1.1.E1 Personal information is invalid, illegible, or incomplete.

Priority:

High

Business Rules:

TBD When business rules are understood.

Assumptions:

Potential volunteers can contact system administrators. Volunteers provide accurate personal information to the best of their ability. It is the job of system administrators to create new volunteer profiles.

Other Information:

 None

Use Case 4

ID and Name:

UC-4 Approve New Volunteer

Author:

Bre Mayall

Date Created:

18/10/2026

Primary Actor:

Volunteer Administrator

Secondary Actors:

Background Check System (BCS); Police Officer (for manual approval); certificate verification source (when applicable)

Description:

The Volunteer Administrator reviews a new volunteer’s application and approves it after the required screening, background check, and (when applicable) educational certificate verification are complete.

Trigger:

The Volunteer Administrator selects a new volunteer profile for approval.

Preconditions:

PRE-1. The administrator is authenticated and authorized to approve volunteers.
  PRE-2. The volunteer profile has been submitted, and initial screening is complete.
  PRE-3. The required background-check result, including any required police approval, has been received.
  PRE-4. Educational certificates have been verified if the volunteer will teach young children.

Postconditions:

 POST-1. The volunteer’s status is saved as Approved.
  POST-2. The approval decision is recorded in the VMS.

Normal Flow:

1.     Administrator opens the list of new volunteer registrations.

2.     VMS displays volunteer profiles and their screening/check statuses.

3.     Administrator selects a volunteer whose required checks are complete.

4.     VMS displays the volunteer’s profile and verification results.

5.     Administrator selects Approve.

6.     VMS validates that all required checks are complete and saves the approval.

7.     VMS updates the volunteer status to Approved and confirms the result.

Alternative Flows:

1.    Certificate verification applies (branches from 3): If the volunteer will teach young children, the administrator confirms the educational certificates are verified before approving; then continue at 5

2.    Further review needed (branches from 4): The administrator does not approve the application and leaves it pending for further review.

Exceptions:

E1 — Background check pending or incomplete: VMS prevents approval and displays the outstanding check status

E2 — Required certificate verification missing: VMS prevents approval when the volunteer will teach young children.

E3 — Save/network failure: VMS reports that approval was not confirmed and does not show Approved unless the change was successfully saved.

Priority:

High

Business Rules:

No rule identifiers are provided in the supplied requirements document. Applicable rule: a volunteer must pass the required background check before approval; educational certificates must be verified for volunteers teaching young children.

Assumptions:

The Volunteer Administrator is the final approver. BCS performs background checks, with police approval handled manually during working hours. Certificate verification is required only for volunteers who will teach young children.

Other Information:

Only authorized administrators may approve volunteers. The VMS should retain an auditable approval status. If a system or network failure occurs, the approval must not be treated as complete unless the status change is saved successfully

Use Case 7

ID and Name:

UC-7 Generate Daily Report

Author:

Kyle Rougeau

Date Created:

18/10/2026

Primary Actor:

Administrative Manager

Secondary Actors:

 

Description:

Generate a daily report of the forecasted number of cases for the next week.

Trigger:

Automatic (daily)

Preconditions:

None

Postconditions:

POST-1. Report is generated.

POST-2. Report is stored for future access.

Normal Flow:

7.0 Generate a Forecast Report

  1. VMS accesses case report history.
  2. VMS pipes report history to prediction algorithm.
  3. VMS uses algorithm output to generate the report.
  4. Report is stored for future access.

Alternative Flows:

None

Exceptions:

None

Priority:

Low

Business Rules:

TBD

Assumptions:

Case report history exists and is accessible 

Other Information:

None (TBD?)

  1. VMS accesses case report history.
  2. VMS pipes report history to prediction algorithm.
  3. VMS uses algorithm output to generate the report.
  4. Report is stored for future access.

TBD more information is to be added later.
Policies of privacy and security of personal information.
Interfacing with a government system to validate background checks.

The VMS is dependent on a government system to validate volunteer background checks. Said government system is currently under development to be fully automated within the next few months. The VMS could be further delayed if the government system is not complete by that time.
The VMS is assumed to have enough volunteers to handle senior cases. If not enough volunteers are available then senior cases will have less support and might cause a backup of unresolved cases.

children.text: <If relevant, describe how data is acquired and maintained. State any requirements regarding the need to protect the integrity of the system's data. Identify any specific techniques that are necessary, such as backups, checkpointing, mirroring, or data accuracy verification. State policies the system must enforce for either retaining or disposing of data, including temporary data, metadata, residual data (such as deleted records), cached data, local copies, archives, and interim backups.>
<This section provides information to ensure that the system will communicate properly with users and with external hardware or software elements.>

<Describe the logical characteristics of each interface between the software product and the users. This may include sample screen images, any GUI standards or product family style guides that are to be followed, screen layout constraints, standard buttons and functions (e.g., help) that will appear on every screen, keyboard shortcuts, error message display standards, and so on. Define the software components for which a user interface is needed. Details of the user interface design should be documented in a separate user interface specification.>

<Describe the connections between this product and other software components (identified by name and version), including other applications, databases, operating systems, tools, libraries, websites, and integrated commercial components. State the purpose, formats, and contents of the messages, data, and control values exchanged between the software components. Specify the mappings of input and output data between the systems and any translations that need to be made for the data to get from one system to the other. Describe the services needed by or from external software components and the nature of the intercomponent communications. Identify data that will be exchanged between or shared across software components. Specify nonfunctional requirements affecting the interface, such as service levels for responses times and frequencies, or security controls and restrictions.>

<Describe the characteristics of each interface between the software and hardware (if any) components of the system. This description might include the supported device types, the data and control interactions between the software and the hardware, and the communication protocols to be used. List the inputs and outputs, their formats, their valid values or ranges, and any timing issues developers need to be aware of. If this information is extensive, consider creating a separate interface specification document.>

<State the requirements for any communication functions the product will use, including e-mail, Web browser, network protocols, and electronic forms. Define any pertinent message formatting. Specify communication security or encryption issues, data transfer rates, handshaking, and synchronization mechanisms. State any constraints around these interfaces, such as whether e-mail attachments are acceptable or not.>

<Specify any requirements regarding characteristics that will make the software appear to be “user-friendly.” Usability encompasses ease of use, ease of learning; memorability; error avoidance, handling, and recovery; efficiency of interactions; accessibility; and ergonomics. Sometimes these can conflict with each other, as with ease of use over ease of learning. Indicate any user interface design standards or guidelines to which the application must conform.>

<State specific performance requirements for various system operations. If different functional requirements or features have different performance requirements, it's appropriate to specify those performance goals right with the corresponding functional requirements, rather than collecting them in this section.>

<Specify any requirements regarding security or privacy issues that restrict access to or use of the product. These could refer to physical, data, or software security. Security requirements often originate in business rules, so identify any security or privacy policies or regulations to which the product must conform. If these are documented in a business rules repository, just refer to them.>

<Specify requirements that are concerned with possible loss, damage, or harm that could result from use of the product. Define any safeguards or actions that must be taken, as well as potentially dangerous actions that must be prevented. Identify any safety certifications, policies, or regulations to which the product must conform.>

<Create a separate section in the SRS for each additional product quality attribute to describe characteristics that will be important to either customers or developers. Possibilities include availability, efficiency, installability, integrity, interoperability, modifiability, portability, reliability, reusability, robustness, scalability, and verifiability. Write these to be specific, quantitative, and verifiable. Clarify the relative priorities for various attributes, such as security over performance.>

<Internationalization and localization requirements ensure that the product will be suitable for use in nations, cultures, and geographic locations other than those in which it was created. Such requirements might address differences in: currency; formatting of dates, numbers, addresses, and telephone numbers; language, including national spelling conventions within the same language (such as American versus British English), symbols used, and character sets; given name and family name order; time zones; international regulations and laws; cultural and political issues; paper sizes used; weights and measures; electrical voltages and plug shapes; and many others.>

<Examples are: legal, regulatory or financial compliance, and standards requirements; requirements for product installation, configuration, startup, and shutdown; and logging, monitoring and audit trail requirements. Instead of just combining these all under "Other," add any new sections to the template that are pertinent to your project. Omit this section if all your requirements are accommodated in other sections. >

<Define any specialized terms that a reader needs to know to understand the SRS, including acronyms and abbreviations. Spell out each acronym and provide its definition.
